slides.headline: Sprint lanes example
notes: The same subscription company and the same QHAG as the Kick Off example.
This slide shows the shape of the whole page. The next slides take each block up close.
Priority #1 is done in week 8, so its lane shows Complete from week 9. Its measure of success stays on the QHAG.

artwork.alt: An example 13-Week Sprint Lanes page for the subscription company, weeks 1 to 13 under January, February and March. Company widgets, week by week, each with an owner. Subscription leads and marketing qualified subscription leads, Chris. New subscriptions, Andrew. Activated subscriptions, Jen. Collected payments, Allison. Company priorities, week by week. #1 remove the first 2 days of activation, Jen, done by February 28: 8 weekly steps, then complete. #2 hire the first account executive, Andrew, done by March 15: 10 weekly steps, then complete. #3 move the 100 largest customers to automatic billing, Allison, done by March 31: 13 weekly steps.

slides.title: Split each month’s number across its weeks.
slides.headline: Split each month’s number across its weeks.
notes: The month’s numbers come from the QHAG the team has just set.
The 13 weeks split 4, 4 and 5 across the 3 months.
March is the highest month in the example, yet its weekly number is the lowest. 5 weeks carry it.

artwork.alt: Three rows. A produced number divides: January’s 65 new subscriptions become 16, 16, 16 and 17 across 4 weeks. A longer month spreads further: March’s 75 become 15 a week across 5 weeks. A held number does not divide: a head count of 30 shows 30 in every week.

slides.title: Forecast each company widget, week by week.
slides.headline: Forecast each company widget, week by week.
notes: Each widget keeps its owner from the QHAG. The weekly numbers you count add up to the quarter’s targets.
A weekly number makes the quarter’s target achievable, not just aspirational.

artwork.alt: The company widgets block of the sprint lanes example on its own. It covers weeks 1 to 13, each widget with its owner. Callout: Why: a weekly number shows a miss while there is time to act. Ask: can each owner reach this week’s number?

slides.title: Give each company priority one lane.
slides.headline: Give each company priority one lane.
notes: The lane keeps the owner its priority has on the QHAG.
Lanes belong to company priorities. They never become lanes for a function.

artwork.alt: The company priorities block of the sprint lanes example on its own: three lanes, weeks 1 to 13. Callout: Why: the team sees each week how the priority gets done. Ask: what must be done this week to finish on time?

slides.title: Write one step for every active week.
slides.headline: Write one step for every active week.
notes: A step can be a decision made, a test run, a result verified or a checkpoint. It only has to be real and checkable.
Avoid blank weeks while the priority is active. Mark a priority complete when it finishes early.
A live priority that cannot name its weekly work is too vague, or too small for a lane.

artwork.alt: Lane #1 on its own: remove the first 2 days of activation, owner Jen, done by February 28. January: week 1, steps mapped. Week 2, slowest 2 days found. Week 3, fix chosen. Week 4, welcome flow drafted. February: week 5, tested with 5 accounts. Week 6, team trained. Week 7, new flow live. Week 8, old flow switched off. March: priority complete. Weeks 9 to 13 need no steps.

slides.title: Rocks only, no sand.
slides.headline: Rocks only, no sand.

panels.heading: “Welcome flow drafted”
panels.support: It is real, and anyone can check it.

panels.heading: “Continue working on activation”
panels.support: If the work would happen anyway, it does not belong in a lane.

panels.heading: A rock becomes sand
panels.support: Once the new way is just how you work, it is no longer a priority.

notes: At Rise Vision we called this rocks only, no sand. “Homepage wireframe approved” is a rock. “Continue working on the new website” is sand.
Read each step in your lane and ask: could someone else check that this is done?
Building something new is a rock. Once it is built and running, it is part of how the company operates. It leaves the lanes and makes room for the next rock.

slides.title: Build your sprint lanes.
slides.headline: Build your sprint lanes.
body: Forecast each company widget for all 13 weeks.
Give each company priority one lane. It keeps its owner.
Write one step for every active week.
notes: Start with the widgets, then take the priorities in rank order. The owner of each lane drafts it and the team questions it.
Building the plan together develops the team as much as the plan.
Allow about 45 minutes.
Homework: add each lane’s steps as sub-priorities under its company priority in Metronome.

slides.title: Is the whole plan achievable?
slides.headline: Is the whole plan achievable?
slides.support: Step back and look at every lane together.
body: You have the people to do it.
You have the cash to do it.
The 13 weeks build to the quarter. Numbers you count add up. Cash and head count match week 13.
notes: If the answer is no, change the plan now. Move a step, change an owner or drop a priority.
Lanes show the work. They are not the measure of success. That stays on the QHAG.
From this week, the weekly leadership meeting reviews sprint lane status.
